#122919. Tech Report: Brain scans reveal a surprising pattern in teens who spend more time on screens

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Brain scans reveal a surprising pattern in teens who spend more time on screens

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study of 44 Finnish teens linked more screen time to smaller gray matter volume in a memory region and larger volumes in some other areas.
  • Earlier studies on teenagers and screens have generally associated longer device use with reduced gray matter in the brain.
  • Gray matter is the brain tissue in which the bodies of nerve cells are concentrated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study of 44 Finnish teens linked more screen time to smaller gray matter volume in a memory region and larger volumes in some other areas.

Earlier studies on teenagers and screens have generally associated longer device use with reduced gray matter in the brain.

Gray matter is the brain tissue in which the bodies of nerve cells are concentrated.

That familiar pattern was also observed in a memory region by a team studying Finnish teens aged 16 to 19.

In regions involved in attention and planning, however, more gray matter was found among the heavier screen users.

These results are difficult to interpret because gray matter volume typically decreases as the teenage brain matures.

The research was led by Hannamari Skog, a doctoral researcher at the University of Eastern Finland‘s Institute of Biomedicine.

Her team scanned the brains of 44 teens on a single occasion each.

In a recent development, habits and brain features that occur together can be identified with this design. Proof that screens altered anyone’s brain cannot be obtained from it.

According to recent reports, the participants were recruited from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children study in Kuopio in Finland. They had taken part in that project for eight years.

A total of 277 teens attended the project’s eight-year checkup and 60 of them were invited to the brain study.

Those invitations were extended so that the full range of performance on a sprint test would be represented.

Forty-six teens agreed to participate. Two of them were later excluded when structural brain abnormalities were detected on their scans.

The final sample consisted of 25 girls and 19 boys who each underwent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.

Specialized software estimated gray matter volume in 102 regions of the outer brain and in 10 deeper structures.

Sources indicate that screen use was assessed by questionnaire. Daily hours on phones, tablets, computers, TV and videos were reported by the teens themselves.

The reported average was 9.2 hours per day and about 5.2 of those hours involved phones and tablets.

Individual totals ranged between 2.5 and 19 hours and each figure rested on the teen’s own estimate.

Sources indicate that the content viewed on the screens was not assessed by the questionnaire. Only the number of hours was recorded.

Fitness was measured with a standing long jump and a shuttle run that covered 164 feet (50 meters) in total.

Recent findings suggest that teens who reported more screen time had less gray matter in the medial temporal lobe. This inner part of the temporal lobe is involved in memory and learning.

Sources indicate that the same link was found for time on phones and tablets alone. It appeared on both the left and right sides of the brain.

Age, sex, head size and body fat were taken into account. The links still held.

In all, the team ran 72 statistical tests. With that many tests, a few links can appear by pure chance.

So a correction was applied to the results. The memory region links survived it.

Recent findings suggest that skog’s team had predicted this result. The temporal cortex matures late, they wrote, and is particularly sensitive to environmental influences.

For the authors, the finding raises concerns, because the region is implicated in memory disorders.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” Skog said.

The researchers had also expected teens with more screen time to have smaller frontal regions.

Sources indicate that teens with more screen time had larger volumes in two frontal regions. One helps the brain initiative movements.

According to recent reports, the other is part of the prefrontal cortex. It supports working memory, planning and decision-making.

It has been revealed that total screen time was also tied to a larger area in the occipital lobe. That lobe processes vision.

Time on phones and tablets was linked to larger volumes in two more frontal regions.

“The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog mentioned.

Industry observers note that some researchers split screen time into active and passive kinds. Active use includes problem-solving or interactive play. Passive use means simply watching.

A 2019 study cited by the team made this kind of split. Gaming was linked to a larger prefrontal cortex in that work.

Social media use was linked to a smaller temporal lobe. The Finnish questionnaire did not distinguish between time spent gaming and time spent on social media.

Industry observers note that an earlier analysis from the same Finnish project had a related result. Some working memory scores were higher among teens with more screen time.

A larger region should not be assumed to be a better one. The prefrontal cortex is also one of the last regions to fully mature.

“During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency,” Skog said.

“The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”.

Recent findings suggest that that idea was not tested in this study. Only one scan exists for each teen.

How each teen’s brain changed over time was therefore not recorded.

Larger temporal and frontal volumes had been expected in active and fit teens, but this pattern did not appear.

According to recent reports, the teens reported 92 minutes of physical activity a day on average. More activity was tied to a larger region in the right occipital lobe.

But that link was no longer statistically significant after the correction.

Fitter teens had a larger left parietal lobe. This region helps process sensation and attention.

Better fitness was also linked to smaller volumes in the right hippocampus and one other region.

Neither of those two links remained after the correction, and the authors wrote that both may be chance findings.

Part of the weak result may be explained by exercise intensity, which was not captured by the questionnaire.

The authors wrote that teenagers’ everyday activity may be too light to influence brain volume.

It has been revealed that each teen was scanned just once. So the study can’t show whether screen habits came before the brain differences or after.

The group of 44 was small and not typical of all teens. Most had a parent with a polytechnic or university degree.

No data on sleep or diet were collected. Either factor could explain part of the pattern.

Sources indicate that skog’s team collected the data in 2018 and 2019. Screen habits may have differed then from the habits seen today, the authors wrote.

The survey recorded screen time by device or broad category, but it did not break down how much time teens spent on specific activities.

Those hours could have been spent on games, videos, schoolwork or social media.

Screen-time apps could capture that detail, the authors wrote, and wearable sensors could measure how hard teens exercise.

“The results provide fresh information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog said.

“However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”.

The authors called for larger studies that follow teenagers over years, to clarify whether different kinds of screen use cause differences in the brain.

The full study was published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports.

#122918. Migrating birds may be bringing unusual ticks to Hungary

Migrating birds may be bringing unusual ticks to Hungary

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.
  • Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness.
  • For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.

Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness. They usually live in warm, dry places, but lately they keep turning up in Hungary.

For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.

What they’ve learned so far raises a simple question: are the ticks just passing through, or are they starting to settle in?

At the HUN-REN Centre for Ecological Research in Budapest, Éva Szabó, Gábor Földvári and their colleagues in the Eco-epidemiology Research Group run the project.

Hyalomma ticks usually live in warm, dry parts of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and southern Europe.

Young Hyalomma ticks often feed on birds, including birds that migrate long distances. Adult Hyalomma ticks feed mostly on large animals such as cattle and horses.

The way these ticks feed helps explain how far they can travel. A young Hyalomma tick usually stays on the same animal while it grows.

For Hyalomma marginatum, that’s about three weeks. Ixodes ricinus, the most widespread tick in Hungary, lets go after less than a week each time.

The authors linked the ticks’ spread north to climate change.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control keeps a map of where Hyalomma marginatum has turned up in Europe.

Scientists watch these ticks closely because of a virus some of them carry.

Industry observers note that the World Health Organization names Hyalomma ticks as the main carrier of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The study’s authors wrote that it’s the most important tick-borne virus affecting people.

According to recent reports, how many people get sick from it each year isn’t clear, because many infections cause no symptoms. The authors cited an estimate of 10,000 to 15,000 cases worldwide.

The World Health Organization estimates that 10% to 40% of reported cases in outbreaks are fatal.

A vaccine has seen limited use in Eastern Europe, and no vaccine is widely available. Treatment relies on supportive care.

Hyalomma ticks hunt their hosts instead of waiting on plants. Dragging a cloth through vegetation, the traditional way to collect ticks, doesn’t work well for them.

So the team relies on citizen scientists instead.

The researchers opened a website called TickWatcher in April 2021.

Four years later, they added a free phone app called PragmaTick. People send in a photo of an odd-looking tick, and an expert checks it.

In a recent development, by late November 2025, the website had about 107,000 visits. The app had been downloaded 2,500 times. Volunteers had made 1,014 submissions, and 29 turned out to be Hyalomma ticks.

The app won’t accept a report without a date, a place and a photo.

In the app’s first six months, people sent about as many reports through it as they had sent by email in the four and a half years before.

“Successfully involving the public in research can even help unravel problems like finding a needle in a haystack,” the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that thirteen of the 29 ticks were on horses. Five were on buffalo, two on dogs, one on a donkey and one on a cow, and reports came in between mid-June and the end of October.

Horse owners tend to check their animals closely and ride through grass and woods, which may help explain why horses topped the list, the researchers wrote.

News about the program may also have reached some groups of people better than others.

Even so, the authors concluded that owners of livestock and other large animals are likely more affected than other groups.

Recent findings suggest that three ticks came from people. Four more ticks were crawling with no host, including the one on the kitchen floor.

Industry observers note that most of the 29 were males, 21 in all. One possible reason, according to the authors, is that males may stay on a host longer while they look for mates.

At a buffalo farm near the village of Ágasegyháza, people found four Hyalomma ticks in 2022 and one more in 2023.

Two other finds came from within about 9 miles (15 kilometers) of the farm. One was on a cow in 2021, and the other turned up in a garden near the city of Kecskemét in 2023.

According to recent reports, all 18 ticks that people mailed in tested negative for the virus. The other 11 were thrown away or destroyed by the people who found them.

Earlier studies in Hungary found antibodies against the virus in 10 of 2,700 people tested between 2008 and 2017, and in 11 of 1,905 cattle and sheep tested in 2017.

Antibodies show past exposure, not a current infection, and these tests may also react to related viruses.

The biggest open question is whether these ticks are only passing through or starting to survive and breed in Hungary.

Recent findings suggest that answering that will take time. The team plans to keep collecting reports, with close attention to livestock owners and to places where several ticks have already been found.

For now, the people in the best position to help are the ones already checking their horses and cattle.

Every tick they send in indicates scientists a little more about where these ticks are turning up.

The full study was published in the journal Current Research in Parasitology and Vector-Borne Diseases.

Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept.
  • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Recent findings suggest that her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

It has been revealed that the Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

Sources indicate that the House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds crucial efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#122915. Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)

Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.
  • The Paris Agreement took effect in 2016.
  • That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.

The Paris Agreement took effect in 2016. From 2016 through 2023, an estimated 540,800 people died from heat worldwide each year, on average.

That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.

The share of heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose from 55% to 68%.

A project based at University College London, the Lancet Countdown, produced the figures in its tenth annual report, which tracks 54 measures of how climate change affects health.

It was written by 146 researchers and produced with the World Health Organization. Every death count in it is an estimate from models, not a tally of death certificates.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jennifer Israelsson, a senior research fellow at the Lancet Countdown, said the finding that surprised her most was not a number from the heat data.

It was “the sharp decline in political engagement with the climate-health agenda, despite multiple years with record-breaking temperatures, deadly heatwaves and devastating flooding events across the globe, and the intensification of hurricanes,” Israelsson noted.

Between 2006 and 2015, heat was linked to an estimated 398,400 deaths a year. Between 2016 and 2023, it was linked to 540,800 a year, with a range of roughly 369,000 to 681,000.

Near the end of that stretch came the worst year. Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, and the authors attributed 71.5% of them to human-caused warming.

The researchers attributed an estimated 2.96 million heat-related deaths to human-caused warming from 2016 through 2023.

Annual heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose by an average of 7,400 per year from 2006 through 2015. From 2016 through 2023, they rose by an average of 15,600 per year.

Sources indicate that the researchers used daily temperatures and death records reported at daily, weekly or monthly intervals across 129 countries. They then used models to estimate the global toll.

The second question was how many of those deaths would have occurred in a world with the same weather minus the warming humans have added.

It has been revealed that the authors call the gap between the two the attributable toll. The attribution step is newly introduced to this year’s report, and the ranges around each figure are wide.

In a recent development, heat also keeps people from working. The authors estimate 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, 35% above the average for 2006 to 2015.

The lost income came to $1.07 trillion, about 0.9% of global economic output.

The losses were equivalent to 5% of GDP in countries with a low Human Development Index and 0.5% in countries with a very high index.

Industry observers note that the same decade brought real gains. Investment in clean energy reached a record $2.1 trillion in 2025, 82% more than went into fossil fuels.

The share of electricity from modern renewables rose from 5.5% in 2016 to 13.5% in 2023. Fossil fuels still supplied 80.7% of the world’s energy in 2023.

Where air pollution from fossil fuels fell, the authors counted the benefit. In 75 of 140 countries assessed, cleaner air prevented an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

It has been revealed that air conditioning tells a mixed story. Its use grew from 32% of households in 2016 to 42% in 2024, and the authors estimate it prevented more than 360,000 heat deaths in each of 2022 and 2023.

In countries with a low Human Development Index, only 3% of households had air conditioning in 2024.

Israelsson told Earth.com the single change that would save the most lives from heat is a heat-health action plan.

That means a warning system that reaches hospitals and the public in time, plus measures for cooler buildings and safe working conditions.

She pointed to the Netherlands, which she noted has seen heat deaths fall since it adopted a heatwave plan.

Extreme drought covered 51.8% of the world’s land for at least a month in 2025, the second-highest extent on record after 2023.

Since 2016, the area in drought each year has grown about eight times as fast as it did in the previous decade.

Very heavy rainfall affected an average of 17.2% of the world’s land each year from 2016 through 2025, up from 14.8% in the previous decade.

Such downpours can increase the risk of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.

The number of people affected per storm or flood rose more slowly in countries with health early warning systems.

The annual increase was 8.6% smaller than in countries without those systems.

Sources indicate that whether the acceleration continues is the open question, and the authors wrote as much. The heat figures run only through 2023, and the drought and rainfall trends through 2025.

The authors’ answer is to have climate change formally declared a global health emergency.

Israelsson stated the WHO’s existing emergency mechanism was built for short, acute outbreaks like Ebola and “is not designed for long-term emergencies.”.

A latest instrument with the same kind of roles and responsibilities, aimed at long-term resilience, is needed, she mentioned.

“A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world’s response to them, and in many cases even accelerating,” noted Marina Romanello, the Lancet Countdown’s executive director.

The report was published ahead of the COP31 climate talks.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.

Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Massive Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.
  • Giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers.
  • The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Significant Bang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Massive Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.

Giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers. Now a team has found what looks like two of them, close together and both feeding.

The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Significant Bang.

If confirmed, it would be the closest-spaced quasar pair known from cosmic dawn.

A quasar is the brilliant glow produced as gas falls toward a supermassive black hole. That glow can outshine all the stars in its galaxy combined.

Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, led the study.

Her team thinks pairs like this one may mark places where young galaxies were crowding together, feeding upcoming stars and fast-growing black holes at the same time.

Industry observers note that the researchers lean toward two real quasars. They haven’t ruled out, though, that the fainter one is a copy of the brighter one, made when light bends around a galaxy in between.

“There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” Onorato remarked.

“We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”.

The universe’s first billion years, a period astronomers call cosmic dawn, were busy.

Clumps of dark matter collapsed, galaxies made their first stars, and the first supermassive black holes took shape at the centers of the biggest galaxies.

Galaxies back then often ran into each other, and some merged completely.

When galaxies collide, gas can funnel toward their central black holes. The gas heats up as it spirals inward, producing the light we see from a quasar.

Since galaxies collided so often, astronomers expect plenty of quasar pairs closer together than the width of a typical galaxy.

Recent findings suggest that so why have so few turned up? Part of the problem is timing, since a black hole shines as a quasar for only a short part of its life.

Distance is the other problem. Quasars from cosmic dawn are so far away that they look faint and are hard to detect from the ground. And when two of them are very close together, it’s hard to tell one from the other.

Sources indicate that those hurdles make Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua a rare find. If confirmed, it would be the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn.

The pair’s Hawaiian name was created through the A Hua He Inoa program at the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The University of Hawaiʻi’s Hawaiian Language College, Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani, also took part.

In English, the name means “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.”.

Astronomers found the pair in the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope program that’s taking a census of objects in the early universe.

Emanuele Paolo Farina, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini, leads the survey.

Industry observers note that farina’s team used Webb to split the light of 200 quasars into its colors, point by point. That’s 43% of all the quasars known from this stage of cosmic history.

In a recent development, onorato’s team checked every one by eye. Next to J1602+4228A, a quasar first reported in 2004, they spotted a second, fainter source. No other quasar in the survey had a companion like it.

The faint one, J1602+4228B, is so dim and so close to its partner that seeing it from the ground should have been nearly impossible.

Earlier Gemini observations from a 2017 program had pointed only at the brighter quasar.

The team went back with Gemini North, a telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawaiʻi, and recorded each quasar’s light separately.

“The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” Onorato remarked.

Industry observers note that the brighter quasar’s black hole weighs about 1.5 billion times as much as the Sun. Its partner’s comes in at about 400 million, roughly a quarter as heavy.

As seen from Earth, the two are about 18,100 light-years apart, or about one-fifth the width of the Milky Way.

The two quasars’ light was stretched by almost exactly the same amount on its way here, which means they’re at nearly the same distance from us.

In a recent development, both black holes are pulling in matter near or slightly above the Eddington limit. At that point, light from the falling gas pushes outward about as hard as gravity pulls inward.

Feeding that fast is typical for quasars this early, the researchers wrote.

The fainter quasar also looks redder, a sign that more dust is blocking its light.

Could the second quasar be a copy of the first? A massive galaxy between Earth and a quasar can bend the quasar’s light and make two or more copies of it. Astronomers call this gravitational lensing.

To test the idea, the team looked at light from gas spread across hundreds of light-years around each black hole.

Stars inside a lensing galaxy can distort light from a small area near a black hole, but not from gas spread that widely.

It has been revealed that the light from the gas indicated different patterns in the two spectra. The brighter source showed a stronger signature of gas flowing outward.

The researchers wrote that this difference favors two separate quasars.

Sources indicate that older Hubble images do show a galaxy near the line of sight to the fainter quasar, which could hold the extra dust or act as a lens. Its spread-out look suggests it’s fairly close to us, making strong lensing unlikely.

Even so, the team wrote, spectra alone can’t definitively rule out lensing.

Based on how quasars cluster over larger distances, a pair this close should be extremely rare.

Yet one turned up among the 199 quasars the team searched around. That’s roughly 100 to 1,000 times more clustering than the predictions suggest.

Predictions at such small distances are very uncertain, though, and one pair can’t show whether close pairs are really this common.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” Onorato stated.

“It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#122913. The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.
  • According to recent reports, predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records.
  • In a fresh study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.

According to recent reports, predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records. Evidence from fossil reefs now suggests this basis has been too narrow.

In a fresh study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.

Four reef-building species were examined: elkhorn, staghorn, boulder brain and mustard hill corals.

More potential habitat for 2100 was identified once the fossil records had been included in the models.

The overall decline was not reversed by this additional habitat. Losses of 45% to 100% of suitable habitat were still projected for each species by 2100.

The extent of loss varied by species and by the level of future carbon emissions.

The research was led by Claire Williams at the University of Texas at Austin’s Jackson School of Geosciences.

Two variables were used to build the computer models: sea surface temperature and sea surface salinity.

Water suitability for each coral was estimated by these models. Actual reef growth at any given site was not predicted by them.

In habitat modeling, every recorded location of a species is paired with the water conditions measured there.

Maps of the future ocean are then searched for matching conditions.

Two limitations of models trained on present-day records alone were described by the authors.

Sources indicate that only water conditions found on Earth today can be learned by such models. Locations where a species is currently absent for other reasons are also missed.

According to recent reports, records from a different ocean are supplied by fossils. Caribbean corals have persisted through hundreds of thousands of years of changing conditions.

The fossil period selected here is regarded by researchers as an analog for present-day warming.

Coral occurrence records were obtained from public sources including the Paleobiology Database. Published reef surveys provided further fossil records.

Recent findings suggest that field observations collected in Jamaica between 2017 and 2024 were added by Williams’s team. At least 16 records per period were available for every species.

Fossil data are useful only if a species’ environmental tolerances have remained stable through time.

A closer match between past and present conditions than chance would produce was found for three species.

Industry observers note that elkhorn coral did not reach this statistical threshold. A large overlap between its past and present conditions was still seen.

Extra future habitat was picked up by the fossil-trained models for each of the four species.

In a recent development, as much as 44,200 square miles (114,559 square kilometers) of added habitat was projected for 2100. That is close to the size of Ohio.

No suitable habitat in 2100 was left for elkhorn or mustard hill coral by the modern-only models under high emissions.

Industry observers note that some habitat for both was kept once the fossil data were added. The authors flagged these estimates as highly uncertain.

The two sets of models were framed by the authors as the edges of a likely range.

Under high emissions, models based only on modern records found no suitable habitat for elkhorn or mustard hill coral in the study area by 2100.

Adding fossils revealed some potential habitat for both, though those estimates are highly uncertain.

It has been revealed that heat-stressed corals lose their color in a process called bleaching. Many of them die afterward.

The worst bleaching ever seen in the Northern Hemisphere came after record marine heatwaves in 2023.

In a recent development, two emissions pathways were tested for each coral. Emissions level off near mid-century in one and keep climbing to 2100 in the other.

Habitat was lost by every species on both pathways. The losses grew under high emissions and from 2050 to 2100.

Boulder brain coral is a massive species that can live for a long time. Its losses were the steepest of all four.

Industry observers note that no suitable habitat was left for it by 2100 under high emissions. Elkhorn coral was left with very little.

This clashes with the official threat status that boulder brain coral currently holds.

The species is ranked as vulnerable by the IUCN, the body that tracks extinction risk worldwide.

Sources indicate that elkhorn and staghorn corals sit one level higher as critically endangered species. Boulder brain coral may be more threatened than once believed, the authors wrote.

The largest share of habitat in 2100 was kept by mustard hill coral on both pathways. It is known as a weedy coral. It spreads easily but builds little reef structure.

Reefs made up mostly of this coral are expected to give less shelter to the sea life people rely on.

The models projected the heaviest habitat losses in the southern Caribbean.

All four species had lost their habitat near 10 degrees north by 2100 under high emissions.

A small patch near 15 degrees north was held only by staghorn coral. Most leftover habitat sat close to 20 degrees north.

The Florida Keys, Cuba and the north coast of Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula still held habitat.

Sources indicate that no real northward shift of the corals was detected. The southern habitat is simply lost and not moved.

Getting to the habitat that is left poses another problem for the corals.

Linked communities of mustard hill coral have been recorded more than 1,000 miles (1,700 kilometers) apart.

Elkhorn coral has been documented spreading only about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer).

Today, about 33% to 38% of modeled suitable habitat overlaps existing marine protected areas.

By 2100 under high emissions, the models projected that share would fall for mustard hill and elkhorn corals and rise for staghorn coral.

The models found no suitable habitat for boulder brain coral anywhere in the study area under that scenario.

New protected areas in the northern Caribbean were called for by the authors.

Closer ties between existing reserves were also urged. Mexico’s Sian Ka’an and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary were named as examples.

Reef-dependent regions such as Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles are likely to lose all suitable habitat for the four corals studied by 2100.

It has been revealed that rowan Martindale is a co-author and associate professor at the Jackson School. According to her, those places cannot simply be abandoned.

Local communities rely on reefs for fish and for protection from hurricanes, she added.

What Jamaica has already lost was examined in a second study by Williams and colleagues.

Fossil and living reefs in northeast Jamaica were compared in the companion study.

These fossil reefs formed 125,000 to 130,000 years ago and are now exposed above sea level.

In a recent development, the surveys were therefore carried out on foot. Corals were photographed at intervals along measured transect lines.

Staghorn coral made up roughly half of the fossil coral on the seaward reefs at Navy Island and Dragon Point.

Elkhorn coral accounted for about 40% of the fossil community at Dragon Point and about 10% at Navy Island.

On nearby living reefs, the largely dead branching corals are now covered by algae. Mustard hill coral dominates the surviving coral cover.

Recent findings suggest that only sea surface temperature and salinity were included in the models. Conditions on the seafloor where corals grow may differ substantially.

Nutrient pollution, turbidity and ocean acidification were not considered in this analysis.

It has been revealed that coral disease and the decline of herbivorous reef animals were also excluded. Further habitat loss from these stresses was anticipated by the authors.

Future water conditions in the Florida Keys and along Cuba’s southern coast will be unlike any fossil or modern record.

Those areas are rated suitable by the models, yet corals may be unable to survive there. Future habitat is therefore likely overestimated.

Newer climate projections became available only after the analysis had been completed. A warmer and more saline Caribbean is indicated by them.

Smaller changes are projected for the Yucatán, which may allow suitable habitat to persist there longer.

“Conservation needs to be adaptive and to keep learning new information,” Williams noted.

It has been revealed that fossils from older warm periods could also be incorporated, according to the authors. Unmatched future conditions would then be reduced.

Future research could also apply this method to reefs in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

The full study was published in the journal Conservation Biology.

Industry News: A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations.
  • It has been revealed that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

It has been revealed that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Sources indicate that heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

According to recent reports, in one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

According to recent reports, smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson indicates. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

According to recent reports, as the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, claims Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson states. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

According to recent reports, some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand indicates, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson claims.

Recent findings suggest that there is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

Sources indicate that so instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

In a recent development, pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as massive as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

According to recent reports, once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

In a recent development, but becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

#122910. Tiny reptile found in Wyoming sandstone is a prehistoric ‘dragon’

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tiny reptile found in Wyoming sandstone is a prehistoric ‘dragon’

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neutron and X-ray scans revealed a tiny horned reptile inside Wyoming sandstone, offering a upcoming clue to where its extinct relatives fit on the reptile family tree.
  • In a recent development, about 156 million years ago, the remains of a small horned reptile were buried in river sand in what is now Wyoming.
  • Its remains stayed hidden inside a slab of sandstone until scientists looked through the rock with neutrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neutron and X-ray scans revealed a tiny horned reptile inside Wyoming sandstone, offering a upcoming clue to where its extinct relatives fit on the reptile family tree.

In a recent development, about 156 million years ago, the remains of a small horned reptile were buried in river sand in what is now Wyoming. Its head and body were found apart.

Its remains stayed hidden inside a slab of sandstone until scientists looked through the rock with neutrons.

Inside, they found a species nobody had seen before. Its tiny, almost intact braincase may help settle a long-running argument about where an odd group of extinct reptiles belongs on the tree of life.

The animal also has a name worthy of a heavy metal album cover.

The research was led by the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland and the University of Zurich, together with the Aathal Dinosaur Museum and the Swiss materials research institute Empa.

It has been revealed that in January 2023, PSI materials scientist Pavel Trtik took his three sons to the Aathal Dinosaur Museum near Zurich. The boys loved the teeth and armor.

Their father was more interested in the rock. Trtik works at the PSI Center for Neutron and Muon Sciences. He uses neutrons to see inside solid materials.

On a whim, he left his business card at the front desk with a note: “If you ever have something you want investigated, just get in touch.”.

It has been revealed that ten days later, the museum called. It had a fossil from the United States that nobody could identify.

A museum excavation team had found the fossil in August 2022 at the Meilyn Quarry in Wyoming.

That part of the American West has produced giants such as Diplodocus, Stegosaurus, and Allosaurus.

This find was much smaller. A row of tiny vertebrae showed in the sandstone, and the rest of the skeleton was still buried inside.

It could have been an early snake, a crocodile relative, or a baby dinosaur. Nobody could say which.

Neutrons turned out to be the right tool for the job.

“Neutrons are particularly sensitive to hydrogen,” Trtik explained.

“And hydrogen is also present in hydroxyapatite, a mineral component of bones. This allows us to distinguish the fossilized remains from the surrounding sandstone.”.

The team also made X-ray scans at PSI, at Empa in Dübendorf and at the University of Zurich.

“The two techniques provide different kinds of information,” Trtik said. “Only by combining them can we get the clearest picture.”.

They then sorted, combined, and interpreted tens of thousands of cross-sectional images. Slowly, the animal took shape.

They found pelvic bones, part of a hind leg and a tiny skull with an almost complete braincase. The skull turned out to be the real prize.

The reconstruction highlights a reptile about 45 centimeters long with two horn-like spikes at the back of its head.

Its head and body were found apart, and fine sand buried both before the sand slowly turned to stone.

“It’s difficult to determine why the skull became detached from the torso,” explained Torsten Scheyer, the University of Zurich palaeontologist who co-led the study with Trtik.

“But we cannot rule out the possibility that a larger predator was involved.”.

If a predator did take the head off, it was lucky for science that the skull wasn’t eaten or carried away by the current.

The braincase is less than two centimeters across, and it holds the most key evidence in the whole fossil.

The skull shows that the animal belonged to the choristoderes, a group of long-extinct reptiles. Later members of the group included long-snouted, crocodile-like river hunters, and some of them outlived the dinosaurs.

Paleontologists have argued for a long time about how choristoderes relate to other reptiles.

“The unusual shape of their skull bones has long made it difficult for palaeontologists to determine how they are related to other reptiles,” Scheyer stated.

The newly introduced clue comes from the bones of the inner ear.

“They bear a striking resemblance to those of the so-called crown group of reptiles, which includes all living reptiles,” the palaeontologist explains.

“This could suggest that choristoderes are more closely related to living reptiles than previous fossil evidence indicated.”.

Sources indicate that the little reptile is also a new species. It is the most complete early member of the choristodere group found so far, and the oldest one known from North America.

Scheyer is a big fan of The Lord of the Rings and of hard rock, and both shaped the animal’s name.

“When I looked at the three-dimensional images of the little reptile, with its head possibly torn off, I knew straight away: such a spectacular creature deserves an equally spectacular name.”.

It has been revealed that he called it Meilynodraco amonamarthi. The first part means roughly “Dragon of Meilyn,” after the quarry and the horns on the back of the head.

The second part honors his favorite band, the Swedish melodic death metal group Amon Amarth.

The band took its name from Tolkien, since Amon Amarth is the Elvish name for Mount Doom, the volcano where the One Ring was made and finally destroyed.

The fossil will go on display in early 2027 in “Rock Fossils on Tour,” a traveling exhibition at the Aathal Dinosaur Museum.

“The little dragon will be in excellent firm here, with other spectacular fossils named after famous metal musicians and rock bands,” said the museum director Yolanda Schicker-Siber.

According to recent reports, PSI hopes to scan much bigger fossils in future. A proposed test facility called UFO, short for “UltraFast neutron irradiation for large Objects,” would fit objects up to a meter long.

It is being considered as part of a possible upgrade to PSI’s neutron source.

The study is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • According to recent reports, sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

According to recent reports, sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

According to recent reports, homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

According to recent reports, paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He stated the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

It has been revealed that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

In a recent development, after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker mentioned. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this key position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

According to recent reports, collins stated in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#122907. Hubble caught a spiral galaxy from an angle that hides its arms

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (789 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Hubble caught a spiral galaxy from an angle that hides its arms

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble indicates a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.
  • The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.

Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble indicates a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.

The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.

It has been revealed that the galaxy is NGC 1827. From this angle, the arms that would sweep around its center in a face-on view overlap along our line of sight.

What stands out instead is the structure of the disk itself, from its glowing central bulge to the uneven ribbon of dust that runs through it.

NGC 1827 lies about 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, also known as the Dove.

Hubble captured this view with its Advanced Camera for Surveys, and NASA released the image on October 16.

A spiral galaxy’s disk is wide and relatively thin. Its arms curve through that disk, carrying stars, gas and dust.

When we see the disk nearly edge-on, much of that material appears in a narrow strip.

The central bulge, which extends above and below the disk, gives the galaxy its thicker middle.

It has been revealed that that geometry also makes the dust especially easy to see. Along parts of the disk, we look through enough dust to dim the combined light of the stars behind it.

The resulting dark lane runs in front of the bright bulge, where the difference between the obscured and unobscured regions is easiest to make out.

Recent findings suggest that follow the dust lane away from the center and you’ll see bright blue patches scattered across the disk. NASA identifies them as places where new stars are likely forming.

In a recent development, hot, massive young stars give off intense blue light. They burn through their fuel quickly by stellar standards, so a concentration of them can point to relatively recent star formation.

In NGC 1827, those blue patches sit among dark clouds, where gas and dust provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

The side view makes it difficult to tell which arm a particular patch belongs to.

A knot of blue light that appears close to the center in the image could sit farther out in the disk, somewhere along the same line of sight.

Hubble shows where each feature appears in the image, but its true distance from the galaxy’s center is harder to pin down.

Just left of the galaxy’s bright middle, a star stands out with four sharp spikes.

Industry observers note that it looks close enough to belong to NGC 1827, but it lies between Earth and the galaxy. Its apparent position is a chance alignment.

Those four spikes offer a clue to another kind of structure, this time inside the telescope. They appear when light from a bright point source bends around the supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror in place.

The pattern is especially obvious on this star because so much of its light comes from one tiny point in the image.

Other objects sit much farther away. Look into the dark sky beyond the disk and you’ll find small, faint smudges, some of them distant galaxies.

A single frame brings together a foreground star, a nearby spiral and galaxies deeper in the background.

The portrait came from a Hubble program targeting 260 satellite galaxies around 22 hosts similar to the Milky Way.

These smaller galaxies give astronomers a way to test how well models of the universe describe what happens on the scale of individual galaxies and their neighbors.

Computer models can reproduce many of the broad patterns astronomers see across the universe.

The details get harder to match on smaller scales, where the growth of galaxies depends in part on how gas gathers and how stars affect the material around them.

Looking at many satellite systems gives researchers a broader sample for those comparisons.

Hubble’s sharp view is useful because a galaxy’s overall brightness tells only part of its story.

In this image, the narrow dust lane, bright central bulge and scattered blue patches each give a different view of how its material is arranged.

From another vantage point, the spiral arms might be the first thing we’d notice.

From Earth, the most striking feature is the dark streak down the middle, visible because the galaxy’s own stars light it from behind.

Image Credit: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (Caltech). Image processing by Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America).

#122905. When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (830 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When AI causes harm, a proposed legal framework would trace responsibility through the decisions people made while building, training, and deploying it.
  • When an AI system causes harm, there is often no obvious person to blame.
  • A proposed legal framework argues that courts can use existing law to trace AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and ran the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When AI causes harm, a proposed legal framework would trace responsibility through the decisions people made while building, training, and deploying it.

When an AI system causes harm, there is often no obvious person to blame. Nobody typed the harmful words, and nobody gave the order.

A proposed legal framework argues that courts can use existing law to trace AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and ran the system.

It would assign responsibility based on the decisions that contributed to the harm.

The proposal comes from Martin Hilbert, a professor of communication at the University of California, Davis.

AI agents now trade stocks, initiative holidays, and write complex software. When they go wrong, the damage can be serious.

Earlier this year, OpenAI reported that AI models it was testing gained access to systems at the machine-learning company Hugging Face.

AI chatbots have also been linked to suicides among young people.

Sources indicate that cases like these don’t fit the law neatly. If a chatbot persuades a child to hurt himself, no single person mentioned those words or even chose them.

In cases like these, Hilbert argues, courts could examine which human decisions contributed to the outcome and who could reasonably have foreseen the risk.

Hilbert identifies two approaches that he indicates are a poor fit for AI.

In a recent development, product liability law points at the tech giant that built the model. But AI models learn from enormous amounts of data that the company didn’t create.

Sources indicate that millions of customers also shape how the systems behave. Putting all the blame on the developer ignores most of the people who contributed.

The other route comes from free speech protections and the immunity laws that shield social media platforms.

Hilbert argues that applying those protections to AI-generated output could lead courts to treat the system as if it were an independent speaker, raising questions about whether it should have rights of its own.

It has been revealed that “Courts adapt tools to regulate earlier technologies, but many of these tools were never designed to address AI,” Hilbert mentioned. “The result is a corridor of precedents that might narrow with every ruling.”.

In other words, every ruling made with these ill-fitting tools becomes a precedent, and the legal options may get narrower each time.

Hilbert argues that existing law gives courts a starting point for tracing AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and deployed the system.

“Every AI, without exception, starts with goals that a human defines, and every subsequent step in the AI’s development involves a chain of deliberate human choices,” he explained.

Because people are involved at every step, tracing their choices shows how much each contributed to a given harm. Liability can then be shared out to match.

The test is foreseeability, meaning whether a person knew, or reasonably should have known, that their decision could cause harm.

Hilbert draws on tools from environmental, vaccine, and financial regulation to show how courts might apply this approach.

Hilbert also points out four further gaps in how the law handles AI, and suggests a fix for each.

Recent findings suggest that the first is the tangled supply chain. A model’s developer can blame the company that deployed it, and the deploying company can blame the developer.

It has been revealed that US environmental law faced the same problem with polluted land. Under the “Superfund” program, responsibility for cleanup costs can extend to many parties at once.

Hilbert suggests a similar approach for AI.

The second gap is the burden of proof. Sometimes a harmful outcome can’t be linked to any single decision about how a system was set up.

In those cases, Hilbert suggests that the company should have to show it acted responsibly, and that no reasonable alternative design would have lowered the risk.

That would reverse the usual arrangement, in which an injured person has to prove what went wrong inside a system they can’t see.

Recent findings suggest that the third gap concerns what happens after release. Product liability assumes that a defect existed when the product was sold.

An AI system’s behavior can change after release as developers patch it or people deploy it in newly introduced settings.

Hilbert argues that this calls for ongoing monitoring and a clear definition of what good-faith compliance looks like over a model’s lifetime.

The last gap is speed. Lawsuits take years, and AI changes in months. Dealing with this requires public governance that can keep pace with the technology.

A first step could be to give the industry’s current voluntary safety standards real enforcement.

“It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care,” Hilbert concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
