#122904. Cannabis use disorder is linked to higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Cannabis use disorder is linked to higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.
  • surveys from 2014 through 2023, researchers found no clear evidence that the link grew stronger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.

Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.

Across U.S. surveys from 2014 through 2023, researchers found no clear evidence that the link grew stronger.

It has been revealed that cannabis use disorder is not the same as using cannabis. It means having trouble controlling the habit even when it is clearly causing harm.

The survey measured it with nine yes-or-no questions about the past year.

Tosin Philip Oyetunji, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced, led the study with three colleagues there.

The team pooled ten years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, which the federal government runs every year. After minors and incomplete answers were set aside, 415,861 adults were left.

Among them, 4.0% met the criteria for the disorder. And 4.6% said that in the past 12 months they had seriously thought about killing themselves.

“What we would most like people to understand is that struggling with cannabis use can go hand in hand with mental health challenges that are not always visible,” Oyetunji remarked in an interview with Earth.com.

Adults with the disorder had 1.57 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts. The range around that figure runs from 1.44 to 1.72.

The comparison is adjusted, which matters more than usual here. The model accounted for depression, serious psychological distress and heavier drinking that met the criteria for alcohol use disorder.

The team also controlled for income, education, insurance, self-rated health, religious attendance and whether a person’s state had legalized recreational cannabis.

In a recent development, so the gap isn’t just depression showing up in a different column. Nobody was followed over time, though, so the survey can’t say which came first.

Industry observers note that the team expected the link to strengthen. Cannabis potency has risen sharply since legalization began, and Canadian data had suggested a tightening link.

An earlier national study had also tied cannabis use to suicidal thoughts, intends and attempts.

The researchers found no clear evidence that the link strengthened. In the 2016 and 2022 surveys, the odds ran higher than in the first survey year.

It has been revealed that neither of those two survived the correction the team applied for testing ten years at once. Across the decade, the differences from one survey to the next were too small to rule out chance.

“A public health concern does not have to be getting worse to deserve attention,” Oyetunji noted when Earth.com asked why the link had held while the drug changed.

Sidra Goldman-Mellor, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study’s senior author, put the other half of it plainly.

“People with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that’s not something that is widely understood,” she mentioned.

The disorder was not the only measure that showed the pattern. The survey’s criteria changed partway through the decade, so the team ran the analysis again using how often people used cannabis.

Recent findings suggest that nondaily users had 1.39 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts, compared with people who had not used cannabis at all. Daily or near-daily users had 1.65 times the odds.

“This suggests that patterns of cannabis use may also be crucial to consider when examining mental health, and it raises questions about how the frequency of use relates to suicidal thoughts,” Oyetunji told Earth.com.

The team also split the sample by sex, by age and by race and ethnicity.

Adults with the disorder had higher odds in every one of those groups, and the differences between the groups were too small to call real.

Everyone answered once, so nobody can say which came first. Every answer was also the person’s own account of a year they were remembering.

In a recent development, the study focused on serious suicidal thoughts. The link with cannabis use disorder may differ for suicide intends, attempts or deaths.

According to recent reports, the survey also records nothing about what people were using. Potency, product type and whether someone vaped concentrates are all missing, so the study cannot test the potency question it raises.

Studies of high-THC products disagree anyway. A recent review found strong links between high-THC cannabis and the disorder itself or psychosis, and weaker ones for depression and anxiety.

Craving and withdrawal were left out of the disorder measure so the questions would match across years, which probably undercounts it.

The survey excluded people living in institutions and people experiencing homelessness who were outside shelters.

The authors raise one more possibility. As cannabis use spread, the group meeting the criteria may have shifted toward milder cases.

A shift like that would hold the average down even if nothing had changed for the most severe cases.

Sources indicate that two people can give this survey the same answers. In one of them, cannabis use deepened a crisis. In the other, a crisis drove heavier use.

A single round of questions cannot tell them apart. Researchers would have to follow the same people for years, with the potency and the products written down.

Oyetunji is widening the question rather than narrowing it.

“I want to better understand how these risks overlap, what drives them, and where we may be missing opportunities to help people before they experience serious harm,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that clinics don’t have to wait for that. Someone asking for help with cannabis may be carrying something they have not mentioned, and the authors argue that the right response is to ask.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs.

#122903. Industry News: Movement can change how rapidly you learn from the same visual clues

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Movement can change how rapidly you learn from the same visual clues

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.
  • In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.
  • Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.

In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.

Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.

The advantage appeared when they had to judge the angle and thickness of the stripes together.

In the punching experiment, volunteers kept their lead when they switched to button presses immediately after training.

For sorting tasks that could be solved with explicit rules, bigger movements gave volunteers no clear advantage.

Luke Rosedahl is an assistant professor of biomedical engineering in Florida Atlantic University‘s College of Engineering and Computer Science.

Professor Rosedahl conducted the experiments at Brown University with Yuka Sasaki and Takeo Watanabe.

The 160 participants were young adults recruited around Brown, sorting striped discs in a headset, so how far the result reaches outside a lab is still open.

“We found that larger movements substantially improved learning when people had to recognize patterns by integrating multiple features, but provided no meaningful benefit when people learned categories using explicit rules,” Rosedahl said.

“Even more intriguing, the benefit occurred whether participants swung at the target or punched a separate response box. The movement itself appeared to matter, not whether it directly interacted with what they were learning.”.

Some categories come with a rule. If it has whiskers and meows, it’s a cat. Psychologists call these rule-based categories, and people learn them by testing hypotheses, which is thought to lean on the front of the brain.

Other categories can’t be put into words. A radiologist’s sense that a lesion looks aggressive comes from weighing several features at once, and so does a driver’s read on whether a road is icy.

People learn these by comparing each newly introduced case with ones they’ve seen.

That kind of learning is thought to run through the striatum, a deep brain structure tied to movement and habits.

Both kinds were tested with the same material: gray discs striped at different angles and thicknesses, shown one at a time in a virtual reality hallway.

In a recent development, for the rule-based version, thickness and angle could be judged separately. For the other version, the dividing line ran diagonally through both, so no single feature gave the answer.

It has been revealed that in the first experiment, 80 people each sorted 600 discs into two groups over 12 blocks, with the disc flashing green or red after every answer. Half answered by pulling a controller trigger.

The other half swung a virtual lightsaber and hit the disc.

On the hard, no-rule categories, the swingers pulled ahead by the second block and stayed ahead for most of the session.

On the rule-based categories, the swingers did very slightly worse, by an amount that could have been chance.

A swing takes longer than a button press, and it touches the thing being judged. Either could have been the real cause.

In a second experiment with 80 upcoming volunteers, some punched a virtual response box separate from the disc, while others pulled a controller trigger.

Every disc stayed on screen for 2.5 seconds, however swiftly they answered.

The rule-based task was also made harder, with two rules to discover instead of one, in case the first version had simply been too easy to show a difference.

Punching still helped on the no-rule categories and still did nothing for the rule-based ones. Slower answers went with worse accuracy, not better, so taking extra time wasn’t the reason.

In the final 100 training trials of the task that required combining both features, volunteers who punched got 90.7% of answers right, compared with 81.0% for those who pressed a button.

It has been revealed that then everyone switched. The punchers moved to buttons and scored 89.5%, almost unchanged. The button group moved to punching and scored 83.1%.

Whatever the major movements had built was still there when the movement stopped, which points to better learning rather than a boost at the moment of answering.

The authors can’t say what the arm is doing for the brain, and they noted so. They offered two possibilities.

One possibility is that more effortful movements increase dopamine release in the striatum, which could help reinforce learning.

In a recent development, effortful actions have also been shown to steer attention toward the features that matter. And movement has helped in other corners of learning, the authors wrote, such as writing by hand to learn to recognize letters.

Industry observers note that the selectivity is the clue. If swinging had simply made people more engaged, Rosedahl’s team wrote, both kinds of categories should have improved.

The benefit appeared only when people had to combine visual features, a kind of learning thought to involve motor circuits.

The result also raises a question about decades of earlier work, nearly all of it done with button presses.

Those studies found that no-rule categories are learned slowly and that written instructions on how to perform them don’t help.

The authors suggested that the buttons themselves may have been holding that learning back.

The team didn’t record which hand participants favored, and controllers were handed out in no particular order, so the role of handedness and motor experience is unmeasured.

It has been revealed that other category types, such as rules with exceptions, may respond differently. And everything happened with participants seated and a headset on.

The team wrote that the next studies should test the effect in real training, in fields such as radiology and aviation.

It has been revealed that there, the judgments that can’t be put into words are the ones that take years to learn. Rosedahl framed the stakes in one line.

“Incorporating movement could offer a simple way to improve learning in situations where conventional approaches fall short,” he said.

Whether a bigger swing of the arm can speed up a radiologist’s eye, and not only a student’s sorting of striped discs, is the test that comes next.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#122901. Industry News: Prickly pear cacti generate electricity, and sunlight changes their voltage

Industry News: Prickly pear cacti generate electricity, and sunlight changes their voltage

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.
  • In a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity.
  • When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.

In a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity. A single stem can produce about half a volt.

When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

Recent findings suggest that the trick depends on the unusual way cacti photosynthesize. They store up acid overnight and use it up in daylight.

That turns each stem into something like a small living solar panel.

The work was led by the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC).

Most plants take in carbon dioxide during the day. They open tiny pores in their leaves, let the gas in and use sunlight to turn it into sugar.

The downside is that water escapes through those open pores. In a desert, that’s a costly trade.

Prickly pears and some of their relatives work around this problem. Aloe, pineapple, and dragon fruit use a system called crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM for short.

According to recent reports, these plants keep their pores closed in the heat of the day and open them in the cool of the night. They pull in carbon dioxide while it’s dark and store it as malic acid, the same acid that makes green apples sour.

When the sun comes up, they break the acid down and finish making sugar.

The cactus’s shape provides the second part of the trick. Prickly pear stems are thick and opaque, another way of holding on to water, so photosynthesis happens only in the outer two millimeters or so.

Industry observers note that when morning light hits one side of a stem, that side starts using up its stored acid. The shaded side keeps its acid.

Industry observers note that the result is a difference in acidity across the stem, from one face to the other. That difference creates a voltage, and the researchers tap into it with a wired electrode inserted into the plant.

In effect, the cactus charges overnight and releases the energy during the day.

The idea came from Michael Loik, a professor of environmental studies who has studied cactus physiology and ecology for about 40 years.

“I’ve been obsessed with the plant since forever, it seems,” Loik remarked.

He suspected the cacti could produce electricity. He and Charlie Chesney, then a PhD student in environmental studies, set out to prove it and measure it.

They used cacti in field plots at the UCSC Farm, in greenhouses, and in the lab. Chesney recruited a large group of undergraduates from engineering, the sciences, and the social sciences, and seven of them are now authors on the paper.

“The undergraduate students told me they liked this project so much because it felt whimsical, and like a light-hearted approach to something that is so serious,” said Chesney, who led the project.

“It was a fun way to explore climate solutions that put creativity first.”.

When researchers wired eight stems together, they measured 4.5 volts, three times the nominal voltage of a standard AA battery.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors. The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

Chesney has since graduated. Colleen Josephson, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, is continuing the work with her PhD student John Madden, and they are looking for ways to strengthen the signal.

Sources indicate that the team also wanted to know how weather and growing conditions affect the voltage. The cacti behaved very much like solar panels.

Voltage was much higher in summer than in winter, and through the day it tracked the amount of sunlight.

“Just how closely the voltage aligned with the sunlight conditions was really surprising,” Chesney remarked.

“Comparing winter to summer voltage, the voltage really follows the same pattern of the amount of sunlight throughout the day.”.

There is an upper limit. Too much sunlight and the cactus goes into self-protection mode.

“If it’s too high, then the cactus will start trying to protect itself from a sunburn, which will also decrease the voltage,” Chesney mentioned. “There’s a balance, a mid-range of light that causes the voltage to be higher.”.

Then came the drought test. The team stopped watering some cacti for 15 months.

Recent findings suggest that the plants survived and kept photosynthesizing. Sometimes, they even produced more voltage than cacti that had been watered normally.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is – it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” Chesney mentioned.

A separate experiment led by undergraduate Erin Langness looked at nitrogen, a common fertilizer ingredient.

Nitrogen increased the cacti’s store of malic acid, so they kept photosynthesizing and producing voltage later into the day.

It has been revealed that the team isn’t trying to run homes on cacti. They have something smaller in mind.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors.

As climate change puts more pressure on crops, farmers increasingly use low-power sensors to monitor their fields.

The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

That could be useful on farms that grow prickly pears for their edible pads, called nopales, and their fruit, called tunas.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti where monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” Loik said.

According to recent reports, “This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue. It could be connected to a plant that acts as sentinel, measuring conditions and sending it back to the base station at the farmer’s office.”.

It has been revealed that other CAM plants, such as agave and pineapple, might work too. The researchers note, however, that some of them may not tolerate the wires as well as the prickly pear does.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • Industry observers note that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

Industry observers note that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

Recent findings suggest that “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Sources indicate that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

According to recent reports, the D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

According to recent reports, the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

Latest Update: Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.
  • Diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count.
  • By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.

Diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count. A upcoming study suggests that one of the best ways to follow them may be through a tiny flatworm that lives in their intestines and in the snails they eat.

By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.

They also found a genetic dividing line about 300 kilometers south of where turtle experts had drawn the boundary between two terrapin subspecies.

The study was carried out by researchers from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute and East Carolina University.

The diamondback terrapin is the only North American turtle that lives exclusively in brackish water, in salt marshes and estuaries along the coast. For a long time, people mostly ate it.

It has been revealed that turtle soup was a fashionable dish, and hunting for it drove the species into steep decline until the early 20th century. Then, in 1920, Prohibition banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes.

Demand collapsed, and so did the hunting.

That wasn’t a happy ending, though. Terrapins kept declining because of habitat loss, coastal development, and drowning in crab pots.

It has been revealed that the species is now listed as “vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List. Conservationists want better data on where terrapin populations live and how they’re connected.

But the turtles are secretive and spread out, and catching enough to answer those questions is slow, expensive work.

It has been revealed that the parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. It can’t complete its life without two hosts.

It has been revealed that its eggs pass out in terrapin droppings and are eaten by eastern mudsnails. Inside the snail, the fluke multiplies by cloning itself.

Its larvae then leave the snail’s soft body and form small pearly cysts on the hard plate the snail uses to seal its shell.

When a terrapin eats an infected snail, the fluke grows into an adult in the turtle’s gut and reproduces sexually there.

Sources indicate that this arrangement is what makes the fluke useful. Mudsnails are abundant and easy to collect, and they barely move.

Terrapins are the ones that carry the parasite from marsh to marsh. If the turtles don’t travel, the fluke’s genes don’t travel either. In principle, the parasite’s family tree should trace the turtle’s movements.

“One of the biggest challenges in conserving vulnerable species is understanding how populations are distributed and connected without having to capture and handle large numbers of animals,” said senior author Michael McCoy from FAU Harbor Branch.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an crucial window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins.”.

The team collected mudsnails from Cape Cod in Massachusetts to St. Augustine in Florida and dissected more than 4,000 of them. Infections inside the snails were rare, never reaching 4% at any site.

The cysts outside were far more common, appearing on as many as 74% of snails at some marshes. Altogether, the fluke turned up at 23 of the 29 marshes sampled.

Finds on Cape Cod and in northeast Florida pushed its known range further north and south.

The Wetlands Institute provided the researchers with 38 female terrapins that had been killed by cars in New Jersey.

Seventeen of them carried adult flukes, with up to seven worms per turtle.

Recent findings suggest that from 476 genetic sequences, the team found 102 distinct versions of a stretch of the fluke’s mitochondrial DNA. More than three-quarters of these versions turned up at only one location.

One version dominated the northern marshes, and another dominated the south. The farther apart two marshes were, the more their flukes differed genetically.

In a recent development, that fits what is known about terrapins. The most mobile of them, adult females, have been recorded traveling no more than 8.5 kilometers. If the hosts stay close to home, their parasites become local too.

The most striking result was where the sharpest split fell. Biologists have traditionally drawn the line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin at Cape Hatteras in North Carolina.

It has been revealed that the fluke’s genetic break falls instead between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina, near the state border. That’s about 300 kilometers further south.

Terrapin subspecies were originally defined by their appearance, before genetic tools existed, so the parasite’s data adds to growing questions about where the real boundaries lie.

It has been revealed that the study also turned up something nobody had described before. Most fluke cysts are pearly white, but some had a faint blush or a pink ring around the edge, while others were bright fuchsia.

Industry observers note that they first appeared in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and Latest Jersey, sometimes on the same snail as ordinary cysts. The color is in the cyst wall, not in the larva inside.

The pink cysts didn’t match any genetic group, and the researchers don’t yet know what causes them. One possibility is that they are simply older.

In a recent development, the authors make a broader point. Parasites account for nearly half of all known species, yet they are rarely studied and almost never protected.

According to recent reports, when a host declines, its parasites decline with it. Scientists recently formed an IUCN group dedicated to parasite conservation, and this study adds basic range and diversity data for a parasite that has been almost entirely ignored.

It has been revealed that the team is careful not to overstate the results. The analysis used a single genetic marker, which is inherited only through the mother.

No one has yet compared fluke genetics directly with terrapin genetics from the same marshes, and that test will decide whether the fluke truly mirrors its host.

Counting cysts is also not a straightforward way to count turtles. One earlier study found that cyst numbers explained less than 8% of the variation in terrapin abundance.

“Our results point to an opportunity to look at conservation from a different perspective,” McCoy stated.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them.”.

“Understanding where these parasites occur and how their populations are genetically connected could help scientists identify key geographic divisions and develop better questions about how terrapin populations should be monitored and managed.”.

The study is published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.

In 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of Latest Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.

Recent findings suggest that that’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.

Sources indicate that it also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.

Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.

Industry observers note that next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.

Scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades.

NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.

In a recent development, ice reveals up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.

In a recent development, the area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.

An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana stated.

The ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana mentioned.

Sources indicate that in 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.

Thinning ice also cracks apart. Each upcoming piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.

It has been revealed that in the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.

Sources indicate that “It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”.

Industry observers note that to count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.

On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana mentioned.

It has been revealed that el Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.

Fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.

In a recent development, during the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS. In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.

According to recent reports, then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.

Recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere.

BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040.

NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

Latest Update: Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet.
  • Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface.
  • Satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet. They were short and came near eddies and fronts, hinting the fish check the ocean.

Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface. Every so often, one keeps going.

Satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). Nobody knows why the fish make them.

Industry observers note that A team from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) has now looked at years of tagging data in search of an answer. The dives were short, fairly steady, and most common where surface temperatures varied and the sea surface stood higher. The authors think the fish may be sampling the water column, possibly to help them find their way. The study was published in Marine Biology.

Swordfish live in open oceans around the world, from about 45 degrees north to 45 degrees south. They follow a daily rhythm. By day they stay deep, usually between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet (400 and 700 meters), and at night they rise toward the surface.

That routine follows their food. Huge numbers of small animals live in the ocean’s twilight zone and move up and down each day, and swordfish track them. Like other large predators of the open sea, tuna and swordfish get much of their food from that dim layer.

Swordfish can handle water from about 36 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit (2 to 31 degrees Celsius). They keep their eyes and parts of their body warmer than the surrounding water, which helps them stay deep for long periods.

It has been revealed that the researchers combined data from 34 pop-up satellite tags placed on North Atlantic swordfish between 2003 and 2024. Twenty-three were tagged off the Atlantic coast of Florida, six near the Grand Banks off Canada, three in the southern Sargasso Sea and two in the Gulf of America, also known as the Gulf of Mexico. Twenty-four were probably adults and 10 were probably juveniles.

The tags stayed on for one to six months and logged depth, temperature and light. Together, they covered 3,666 days of swordfish life.

The data came from a partnership with NOAA’s Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

“It wouldn’t have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab,” said Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and an author of the study.

The team flagged 39 days on which a fish went unusually deep for its own normal pattern. On 25 of those days, recorded by 10 tags, the data were detailed enough to confirm a distinct extreme dive.

These dives averaged about 3,250 feet (991 meters) at their deepest point, and the deepest reached roughly 5,460 feet (1,664 meters), more than a mile down. On ordinary days, the fish’s deepest point averaged about 2,090 feet (637 meters).

It has been revealed that A single extreme dive lasted about 45 to 55 minutes on average. When a fish made one such dive in a day, it usually dropped two to three times faster than it climbed back. In one fish’s full-resolution record, it spent between a few seconds and about six minutes at the bottom.

The water at the bottom of these dives averaged about 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8.4 degrees Celsius). On other days, the coldest water the fish met averaged about 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12.1 degrees Celsius).

Most dives started and ended in the twilight zone, during daylight. In 12 of 16 such dives, the fish came back to within about 33 feet (10 meters) of the depth where it began.

The authors weighed seven possible reasons for deep dives, including feeding, escaping predators, saving energy and navigation.

It has been revealed that feeding seemed unlikely. A hunting fish would be expected to linger at depth, but these fish barely paused at the bottom before heading back up. The dives also did not cluster at dawn and dusk, when prey is easiest to reach.

Escape did not fit well either. The descents were steady, about 3.3 feet (1 meter) per second, and the fish behaved normally afterward. Only one dive began and ended near the surface at night, when the authors think predators may be more likely to be around. The authors could not rule out that the two juveniles, which made several dives in a single day, were avoiding predators.

According to recent reports, extreme dives were much more likely where sea surface temperature varied a lot and where the sea surface stood higher. In the team’s model, each extra degree Celsius of temperature variation made a dive about 23 times more likely. These conditions mark swirling eddies, fronts and major currents such as the Gulf Stream.

The authors suggest that crossing into a latest water mass may prompt a swordfish to check what lies below. Short, repeatable dives of the same shape would fit that kind of sampling.

“They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses,” said Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program and now works at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Sources indicate that deeper water could also give a clearer reading of Earth’s magnetic field, which many fish can sense, away from the busy, changing layers near the surface. Some dives happened near seamounts, ridges and magnetic anomalies, but those links were weak, though rough seafloor highlighted a smaller but significant effect. Other ocean travelers are under similar suspicion, as oceanic manta rays also dive deep, apparently not to feed.

In a recent development, the authors stress that their conclusions are inferences. Satellite tag positions carry an average error of about 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 kilometers), and possibly more for deep divers like swordfish. That makes it hard to match a dive to a specific seafloor feature.

It is still unclear how common these dives are among swordfish, and whether they differ between populations or ages.

Swordfish support valuable fisheries, so knowing what steers them could help predict where they go as the ocean changes.

The information was obtained from the study published in Marine Biology and from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

  • It has been revealed that the Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

It has been revealed that the Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

It has been revealed that the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch declared he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Latest Update: A metal detectorist found a Viking sword and rare oval brooches on the Isle of Man, and his father had helped find the island’s only other pair

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man.
  • In a recent development, A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old.
  • The finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man. His father helped find the island's only other pair.

In a recent development, A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old. The objects are believed to come from a double Viking burial.

The finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this. In December 2018, his father, John Crowe, and fellow detectorist Craig Evans found the only other pair of Viking oval brooches ever discovered on the island.

Recent findings suggest that the new collection was declared Treasure by the Isle of Man Coroner for Inquests, and Manx National Heritage confirmed it on November 9. Part of it went on display at the Manx Museum in Douglas two days later.

Sources indicate that the finds date to around AD 900. Besides the sword, the haul includes three bronze brooches, decorated lead weights, fragments of bronze balance scales, a bronze ladle and an axehead.

Fellow detectorist Rhett Britton helped with the search. He found the axehead, part of the scales and other iron objects.

According to recent reports, the sword is the thirteenth Viking sword found on the island. About two-thirds of it survives. X-rays revealed fine silver inlay and twisted silver wire on parts of its hilt, and only two other Manx Viking swords carry comparable decoration.

Industry observers note that it is broken, probably on purpose as part of the burial ritual. Some more damage happened later, while it lay in the ground.

Two of the brooches are oval and decorated with interlocking animals, a distinctive feature of Viking art. Brooches like these were usually worn by women.

Industry observers note that the pair found by John Crowe and Craig Evans in 2018 dates to around AD 900 to 950. The new pair could be about 50 years older, which would make it potential evidence of the earliest known female Viking Age burial on the Isle of Man.

Oval brooches were particularly common in the Viking homelands and are seen almost as national dress.

In 2020, Manx National Heritage said their absence from the island until the 2018 find had led to theories that only men from Scandinavia settled there in the early Viking Age.

It has been revealed that the third brooch was originally gilded. It has spiral decoration and a glass center, and it is the first of its kind found on the island.

Recent findings suggest that jewelry typically associated with women, found alongside a sword traditionally associated with men, raises a possibility. The objects may come from a double burial, or from separate graves of the same period.

The site was disturbed at some point over the last thousand years, so the exact circumstances are still uncertain.

At the site of the 2018 brooches, archaeologists from York Archaeological Trust carried out a small excavation but found no grave.

Recent findings suggest that the decorated lead weights and bronze scales would have been used to weigh precious metals and coins during trade. The weights are the first of their type found on the Isle of Man.

Silver and coins also turn up in hoards across the Viking world, like a buried 10th-century hoard that revealed vast Viking trade networks.

Recent findings suggest that one weight carries a bronze fitting, possibly taken from a small chest or a religious object. Its art style is typical of Britain and Ireland at the time, which suggests the settlers reused objects from other cultures.

The ladle, perhaps used at feasts or ceremonies, is another type of object never recorded before on the island.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” mentioned Allison Fox, Curator for Archaeology at Manx National Heritage.

Industry observers note that crowe chose not to clean the objects and handed them over in the state they came out of the ground. That kept traces of evidence that could otherwise have been lost.

Recent findings suggest that his father and Evans did the same in 2018. In 2020, Fox remarked this mattered because the brooches were fragile and small fragments of textiles from the clothes the woman was buried in might still survive.

Sources indicate that this time, before conservation began, the radiology team at Manx Care scanned the objects. The scans looked beneath layers of compacted soil and guided the conservator in uncovering and preserving the objects.

Detectorists elsewhere have made similar finds, such as the hiker with a metal detector who found a Viking treasure hoard and the detectorist who found Finland’s largest Viking Age silver hoard.

Recent findings suggest that manx National Heritage has not mentioned exactly where the objects were found, only that the landowner cooperated. It also has not given a date for the discovery.

Conservation and research are still underway, and they may reveal more about who owned these objects. Several of them are the first of their kind on the island, so they offer a rare look at early Viking settlement, burial and daily life there.

Visitors can see a selection of the finds in the Viking Gallery of the Manx Museum.

The information was obtained from Manx National Heritage and its 2020 announcement on the earlier brooches.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

According to recent reports, in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a substantial, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

It has been revealed that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she indicates. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this upcoming climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

Recent findings suggest that but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

It has been revealed that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

Recent findings suggest that but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, indicates Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

It has been revealed that as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

Recent findings suggest that on February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

Recent findings suggest that “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

It has been revealed that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

Sources indicate that the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

According to recent reports, gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

It has been revealed that he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves claims.

Recent findings suggest that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier notes. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

Recent findings suggest that california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier claims. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Sources indicate that those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

In a recent development, such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a significant boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

According to recent reports, it’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, notes Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

According to recent reports, as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

It has been revealed that then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

According to recent reports, those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Recent findings suggest that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, notes she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

Sources indicate that “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she notes. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

Sources indicate that but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

November’s full moon on Nov. 24 is the first of three supermoons in a row, and it will pass close to the Pleiades

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.
  • The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.
  • In a recent development, the Moon turns full at 9:53 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.

The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.

In a recent development, the Moon turns full at 9:53 a.m. EST (14:53 UT), the U.S. Naval Observatory calculates. That is midmorning on the East Coast, so the best views come before dawn and again that evening.

Before sunrise, the nearly full Moon will pass close to the Pleiades star cluster, while Mars and Jupiter shine in another part of the sky.

Sources indicate that the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, so its distance from Earth changes. At its closest point, called perigee, it is about 226,000 miles (363,300 kilometers) away, and at its farthest about 251,000 miles (405,500 kilometers).

It has been revealed that A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with that closest approach, NASA explains. The word is not an official astronomical term and typically describes a full Moon within at least 90 percent of perigee.

Such a Moon can appear up to 14 percent bigger and 30 percent brighter than the faintest full Moon of the year.

Industry observers note that “It might be hard to detect a supermoon visually, but it does have an effect on Earth,” the space agency’s page states. A Moon at perigee can cause higher tides than usual.

Measured against an average full Moon, the gain is smaller: up to 7 percent larger and 15 percent brighter, the Royal Observatory Greenwich notes.

When it turns full, the Moon will be roughly 224,200 miles (360,800 kilometers) from Earth. That is around 12,400 miles (20,000 kilometers) closer than average, by the Greenwich astronomers’ figures.

Recent findings suggest that perigee itself arrives about 30 hours later, on November 25 at 4:01 p.m. EST. The Moon will then be 223,400 miles (359,567 kilometers) away, a government almanac from Land Information Fresh Zealand demonstrates.

December’s full Moon falls on December 23 at 8:28 p.m. EST. Perigee follows about seven hours later at 221,800 miles (356,903 kilometers), the closest of the three.

The third full Moon comes on January 22, 2027, at 7:17 a.m. EST. Perigee occurs the previous afternoon, at 222,200 miles (357,530 kilometers).

According to recent reports, measured at perigee, November’s supermoon is therefore the most distant of the trio. It follows the Beaver Moon of November 2025.

It has been revealed that U.S. Naval Observatory rise and set tables put moonset in Upcoming York at 7:05 a.m. EST, 12 minutes after sunrise. In Los Angeles, the Moon sets at 6:49 a.m. PST.

Early risers should look low in the west, toward Taurus, the constellation that holds the Pleiades.

Industry observers note that the International Occultation Timing Association lists that date among the Moon’s 2026 passages over the cluster. In an occultation, the Moon moves in front of a star and hides it.

The listing does not rank it among the year’s best passages. Bright moonlight will also make the cluster’s faint stars harder to pick out.

Higher up, Mars and Jupiter have been neighbors all month. They appeared about 1.2 degrees apart on the mornings of November 15 and 16, slightly more than two full Moon widths.

In a recent development, jupiter is the brighter of the two, and Mars has a reddish tint. Binoculars or a low-powered telescope, under 40x magnification, give a closer look.

The planets have since drifted apart and stand high in the south before dawn, near Regulus, the brightest star in Leo.

Such Mars and Jupiter pairings recur every 2 to 2.5 years on average, by the Royal Observatory’s count. Mars circles the Sun faster and laps Jupiter in the night sky.

Recent findings suggest that the second chance comes at dusk. “Look east around sunset to watch it rise,” NASA’s November skywatching guide advises.

According to recent reports, “It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion,” the guide adds. The effect is common to any full Moon.

Moonrise in Upcoming York is at 4:16 p.m. EST, 16 minutes before sunset. Los Angeles sees the Moon come up at 4:43 p.m. PST, two minutes ahead of the Sun’s setting.

Bill Ingalls, then NASA’s senior photographer, shared supermoon photography tips in 2016.

According to recent reports, “Don’t make the mistake of photographing the moon by itself with no reference to anything,” Ingalls noted. “I’ve certainly done it myself, but everyone will get that shot.”.

He suggested including a local landmark to give a photo a sense of place. For phone cameras, he advised holding a finger on the Moon to lock focus, then sliding it to adjust exposure.

In a recent development, beaver Moon is a nickname for November’s full Moon. The name draws on several traditions and folklore in Native American and European culture.

Industry observers note that one explanation is that beavers spend November fortifying their dams and stocking food for winter. The month was also the season to trap the animals for their thick, winter-ready pelts.

“There is disagreement over the origin of November’s ‘Beaver Moon’ name,” the Royal Observatory’s monthly highlights state.

The word “supermoon” was coined in 1979, the same 2024 NASA post says.

The information was obtained from NASA’s skywatching guide.

Dan Bartlett from June Lake, California.

Asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In this image, the tail spans more than 35′, or wider than the Full Moon.

  • Industry observers note that the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll patch this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

It has been revealed that sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum.

Sources indicate that stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.
